did.abstract: The Wallace House Center for Journalists is an organization within the University of Michigan that administers the Knight-Wallace Fellowships and the Livingston Awards. This collection consists of correspondence, administrative records, and publications relating to the activities and functions of the Wallace House, with emphasis on the fellowship program.

accessrestrict.p: Restricted access in part. Interview files within the Fellows records series contain personnel records, and are restricted for 30 years following their creation.

p.emph: Access Restrictions for University of Michigan Records

blockquote.p: University records are public records and once fully processed are generally open to research use. Records that contain personally identifiable information will be restricted in order to protect individual privacy. Certain administrative records are restricted in accordance with university policy as outlined below. The restriction of university records is subject to compliance with applicable laws, including the Michigan Freedom of Information Act.

Categories of Restricted Records
Personnel-related files, including search, review, promotion, and tenure files, are restricted for thirty (30) years from the date of their creation.
Restricted files are indicated in the contents list of the collection’s finding aid with a restriction note indicating the restriction type and the date of expiration.

For further information on the restriction policy and placing Freedom of Information Act requests for restricted material, consult the reference archivist at the Bentley Historical Library (bentley.ref@umich.edu) or the University of Michigan Freedom of Information Office website (https://foia.vpcomm.umich.edu/).

acqinfo.p: Donated by the Wallace House Center for Journalists (donor no. 11568) in August 2016 and July 2018.

arrangement.p: The collection is arranged into 7 series: Organizational History, Correspondence, Financial and development records, Publications, Conferences, Humor at Michigan program, and Fellows records.

bioghist.p: The Wallace House Center for Journalists is an organizational unit within the University of Michigan that administers the Knight-Wallace Fellowships and the Livingston Awards. The namesake Wallace House property was donated by renowned journalists Mike Wallace and his wife, Mary, in 1992. The organization began in 1973 with just the fellowship program, which provides mid-career reporters, editors, photographers, producers, editorial writers and cartoonists with educational and professional development opportunities. Fellows attend seminars, pursue independent study, and engage in international travel. The fellowship was initially funded through a National Endowment for the Humanities grant, but it has since shifted to being financed through its own endowment. The fellowship has undergone several name changes in its history: The National Endowment for the Humanities Journalism Fellowship (1973), Journalists in Residence (1984), Michigan Journalism Fellowship (1987), Knight-Wallace Fellowship (2002, following substantial donations from the Knight Foundation and Mike Wallace). Program directors include Ben L. Yablonky (1973-1980), Graham B. Hovey (1980-1986), former fellow Charles R. Eisendrath (1986-2015), and former fellow Lynette Clemetson (2015-present). The Livingston Awards are awards given to American journalists under the age of 35. It is the largest general reporting prize in America, and it is popularly referred to as the "Pulitzer for the young." Winners have included notable journalists such as Michele Norris, Christiane Amanpour, David Remnick, Ira Glass, Tom Ashbrook, Michael S. Schmidt, and Ronan Farrow. The awards were established in 1981 by American fashion designer Mollie Parnis Livingston in honor of her son, Robert, and were first directed by Charles R. Eisendrath. In 2015, the Knight-Wallace Fellowships and Livingston Wards were jointly rebranded as Wallace House.

relatedmaterial.p: The Bentley Historical Library houses the following related collections: Charles R. Eisendrath papers, Mike Wallace papers, Mike Wallace CBS 60 Minutes papers.

scopecontent.p: This collection consists of correspondence and administrative records relating to the activities and functions of the Wallace House Center for Journalists. Significant focus is placed on the administration of the Knight-Wallace Fellowship (previously known as the NEH Journalism Fellowship and the Michigan Journalism Fellowship). Included are administrative correspondence, financial and development records, publications, and material related to conferences, events, and initiatives run by the organization.

userestrict.p: Copyright is held by the Regents of the University of Michigan but the collection may contain third-party materials for which copyright is not held. Patrons are responsible for determining the appropriate use or reuse of materials.

scopecontent.p: This series consists of records that provide context for the administration and structure of the organization throughout its lifespan. Included is information regarding a documentary on the organization during its inaugural director's tenure, a file on the 1980 search for a new director, the Livingston Awards for Young Journalists, organizational restructuring from 1886-1988, and travel itineraries.

This series consists of administrative correspondence throughout the life of the organization, arranged chronologically. Notable correspondents include directors Ben Yablonky, Graham Hovey, and Charles Eisendrath; as well as other employees including Margaret DeMuth and deputy director Wendy Palms. Correspondence is filed by incoming and outgoing as well as by category, including correspondence from the broader U-M campus and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

This series consists of materials relating to the funding and budgeting of the Wallace House. These include proposals and reports to the National Endowment for the Humanities, development files for various other foundations, budgets, and materials related to fundraising. A significant portion of the records pertain to the Wallace House's working relationship with the Kellogg Foundation. Also included are records relating to the purchase, dedication, and events of the Wallace House property.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: Humor at Michigan (HAM) was a program started by Charles Eisendrath in 2003 following the immense success of a fellow-organized seminar on the mechanics of humor, given by New Yorker cartoon editor, Bob Mankoff. The program was jointly led by Charles Eisendrath; Richard Gonzalez, Chair of the Department of Psychiatry; John Greden, Director of the Depression Center; and Daniel Herwitz, Director of the Institute for Humanities. HAM supported public lectures and research by Bob Mankoff on various aspects of humor, incorporating interdisciplinary methods in the humanities and cognitive psychology.

scopecontent.p: This series consists of administrative records, publicity, and correspondence related to the Humor at Michigan program.
